data.note: import: sentence-boundary titles, body text, globs, prose deps

data.claim: scan_todos only reads **Globs:**/**Needs:** annotation lines, so prose paths and 'Requires X' never reach globs/needs
data.falsifier: a task whose text names `src/a.py` and 'Requires OPIK.3' already imports with those globs/needs
data.mechanism: no code reads the paragraph text for paths or dependency phrases
data.probe: uv run pytest tests/test_import_prose_globs_needs.py on unfixed code

chunk_findings.detail: The dependency extraction takes every token that looks like a known id anywhere in the 200 characters that follow the keyword, with no sentence/clause boundary and no check that the id is actually the object of the dependency. `_ID_TOKEN.findall(m.group(1))` over `.{0,200}` therefore harvests ids from unrelated following sentences. Concretely, for a paragraph such as `"Reworks the importer. Requires no new config. Related work is tracked in 160.C.2."`, `_PROSE_DEP` matches `Requires`, group(1) is `" no new config. Related work is tracked in 160.C.2."`, and `160.C.2` (a valid id in `known`) is appended to `task.needs` — even though the sentence says nothing is required. Because `_add_prose_needs` mutates `task.needs` directly and the code's own docstring states an unmet need "would read as unmet and block the task for good", this turns a harmless mention into a permanent phantom blocker. The `known`-membership guard only prevents ids nobody wrote; it does nothing about ids written in a non-dependency role.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer.py:_prose_needs

chunk_findings.detail: Line/position suffixes on backticked paths are kept, producing globs that can never match, so the very protection the change promises (conflict detector coverage of tasks with no globs) is silently lost for exactly the reference style the bug report uses. `raw.rstrip(".,;:")` only strips *trailing* punctuation, so `` `ddflow/services/importer.py:1219` `` (the form cited in the intent as `importer.py:1219,1580`) contains `/` and is appended verbatim as glob `ddflow/services/importer.py:1219`. That is not a path git/pathspec globbing will ever resolve to `ddflow/services/importer.py`, so the task still has an effective glob set of ∅ and remains invisible to the conflict detector — the failure mode the change was supposed to fix, now with a non-empty-but-dead glob list that also looks correct in the import plan.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer.py:_prose_globs

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test for imp-titles-truncated-no-text never asserts on `title` or `body`. The bug's primary symptom is `importer.py` cutting titles at 120/140 chars (mid-sentence or leaving an unclosed backtick) and writing a bare "Imported from file:line" body, yet every task line in the fixture is under ~90 characters, contains no unclosed backtick, and the only fields inspected are `globs` and `needs`. Concretely: revert the title/body half of the fix (restore the 120-char cut and the bare body) and this suite is still green — the test only fails on the globs/needs half. A regression test that cannot fail on the truncation it is filed under leaves that behaviour unprotected; the fixture needs at least one task whose first paragraph exceeds 140 chars and ends inside a backticked path, with `assert t["..."].title == ...` and an assertion that the body carries the full first paragraph.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_import_prose_globs_needs.py:14 (TODO fixture) / `_found`

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to cover 'Requires/Depends on/Needs <id>' but only one of the three forms is actually discriminated. `OPIK.9`'s prose is "Requires OPIK.3 and Needs the stratum (OPIK.3); Depends on NOPE.7 which nobody wrote." — the expected `["OPIK.3"]` is already produced by the bare "Requires OPIK.3", so deleting support for the descriptive parenthetical form ("Needs the stratum (OPIK.3)"), which is exactly the "Needs the retrieval-miss stratum (160.C.2)" symptom named in the intent, leaves the assertion passing. The "Depends on" branch is likewise never proven, because its only occurrence targets `NOPE.7`, which is removed by the known-id filter the same test asserts. Add a task whose *only* dependency signal is the parenthetical form (e.g. "Needs the shutdown drain (OPIK.3)") and one whose only signal is "Depends on OPIK.10", so each keyword path has a failing witness on its own.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_import_prose_globs_needs.py:40 `test_prose_requires_becomes_a_need_only_for_a_known_id`

chunk_findings.detail: The test name promises that commands are not harvested as globs, but the only command in the fixture is `pytest -q`, which contains neither `/` nor `.`. Any implementation that merely keeps backticked spans containing a slash or a dot passes this, so the "commands do not" half of the name is untested. A command that carries a path (`` Run `python ddflow/cli.py import` ``) is the input that would actually distinguish a path-shape filter from a keyword filter; without it the claim in the test name is vacuous.

chunk_findings.detail: The split pattern includes `:`, but the colon is exactly what separates the keyword from its ids in a very common prose form. For a bullet such as `- [ ] **OPIK.15** Depends on: OPIK.10 for the schema.`, `_PROSE_DEP` matches only `Depends on`, so `m.group(1)` is `": OPIK.10 for the schema."`. `re.split(r"[.;:]\s", ": OPIK.10 for the schema.", maxsplit=1)` matches the `": "` at the start and returns `["", "OPIK.10 for the schema."]`, so `clause` is the empty string and `_ID_TOKEN.findall` yields nothing → `needs == []`. The previous code (`_ID_TOKEN.findall(m.group(1))`) found `OPIK.10`, so this is a regression, and the same happens for `Needs: OPIK.3`, `Requires: OPIK.9`, `Blocked by: OPIK.7`. The added tests never use the `Keyword: <id>` form, so nothing catches it.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/services/importer.py `_prose_needs` clause split (`clause = re.split(r"[.;:]\s", m.group(1), maxsplit=1)[0]`)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer.py `_prose_needs` clause split (`clause = re.split(r"[.;:]\s", m.group(1), maxsplit=1)[0]`)

chunk_findings.detail: Because `_PROSE_DEP` captures `.{0,200}` greedily and `.` does not cross newlines, the first keyword match swallows the entire rest of the line, and `finditer` resumes only after it. Combined with taking only `[0]` of the split, every dependency phrase after the first on the same line is dropped. Input `- [ ] **OPIK.16** Requires OPIK.3. Needs OPIK.10.`: the single match starts at `Requires`, `m.group(1)` is `" OPIK.3. Needs OPIK.10."`, the split at `". "` yields `clause == " OPIK.3"`, and `Needs OPIK.10` is never examined as a match at all — `needs == ["OPIK.3"]`. Before the change, `_ID_TOKEN.findall` over that same group returned both `OPIK.3` and `OPIK.10`. So a genuine `Needs <known-id>` phrase is silently lost (the very failure the feature is meant to prevent: the conflict detector cannot protect that task), while the test suite only covers phrases separated by newlines (`OPIK.9`) where `finditer` can restart.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/importer.py `_prose_needs` (finditer consumption + clause truncation)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new clamp `clause = re.split(r"[.;:]\s", m.group(1), maxsplit=1)[0]` is not applied to a sentence — `_PROSE_DEP`'s `(.{0,200})` capture is up to 200 characters of the *paragraph* after the keyword, and `finditer` skips everything the match consumed. Two concrete inputs go wrong:

1. Keyword directly followed by a colon. For `- [ ] **OPIK.20** Needs: OPIK.3.` (OPIK.3 declared earlier, so it is in `known`), `m.group(1)` is `": OPIK.3."`; `re.split(r"[.;:]\s", ...)` splits at the colon because it is followed by a space, so `clause` becomes `""`, `_ID_TOKEN.findall("")` returns nothing, and `OPIK.20.needs == []`. Before this change the same input produced `needs == ["OPIK.3"]` (the old code scanned all of `m.group(1)`), so this is a regression: `Requires: OPIK.3`, `Needs: OPIK.3` and `Depends on: OPIK.10` are all silently dropped.

2. A second dependency phrase later in the same paragraph is swallowed by the first match. For `- [ ] **OPIK.21** Depends on OPIK.3. Needs OPIK.5.`, the match on `Depends on` consumes `" OPIK.3. Needs OPIK.5."` (no newline, under 200 chars); the clamp keeps only `" OPIK.3"`, and because `finditer` resumes *after* the consumed match, the `Needs OPIK.5` keyword is never seen again — `needs == ["OPIK.3"]`, `OPIK.5` is lost. Pre-change both ids were reported.

Both cases silently under-report needs — the exact failure class this change exists to fix (a missing need means the task is never marked blocked and the conflict detector cannot protect it), and neither case is covered by the added tests, which only exercise a later sentence that contains no dependency keyword (`Related: see OPIK.3`).

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test for imp-titles-truncated-no-text never asserts on `title` or `body`. The bug's primary symptom is `importer.py` cutting titles at 120/140 chars (mid-sentence or leaving an unclosed backtick) and writing a bare "Imported from file:line" body, yet every task line in the fixture is under ~90 characters, contains no unclosed backtick, and the only fields inspected are `globs` and `needs`. Concretely: revert the title/body half of the fix (restore the 120-char cut and the bare body) and this suite is still green — the test only fails on the globs/needs half. A regression test that cannot fail on the truncation it is filed under leaves that behaviour unprotected; the fixture needs at least one task whose first paragraph exceeds 140 chars and ends inside a backticked path, with `assert t["..."].title == ...` and an assertion that the body carries the full first paragraph.

chunk_findings.detail: The split pattern includes `:`, but the colon is exactly what separates the keyword from its ids in a very common prose form. For a bullet such as `- [ ] **OPIK.15** Depends on: OPIK.10 for the schema.`, `_PROSE_DEP` matches only `Depends on`, so `m.group(1)` is `": OPIK.10 for the schema."`. `re.split(r"[.;:]\s", ": OPIK.10 for the schema.", maxsplit=1)` matches the `": "` at the start and returns `["", "OPIK.10 for the schema."]`, so `clause` is the empty string and `_ID_TOKEN.findall` yields nothing → `needs == []`. The previous code (`_ID_TOKEN.findall(m.group(1))`) found `OPIK.10`, so this is a regression, and the same happens for `Needs: OPIK.3`, `Requires: OPIK.9`, `Blocked by: OPIK.7`. The added tests never use the `Keyword: <id>` form, so nothing catches it.

chunk_findings.detail: Because `_PROSE_DEP` captures `.{0,200}` greedily and `.` does not cross newlines, the first keyword match swallows the entire rest of the line, and `finditer` resumes only after it. Combined with taking only `[0]` of the split, every dependency phrase after the first on the same line is dropped. Input `- [ ] **OPIK.16** Requires OPIK.3. Needs OPIK.10.`: the single match starts at `Requires`, `m.group(1)` is `" OPIK.3. Needs OPIK.10."`, the split at `". "` yields `clause == " OPIK.3"`, and `Needs OPIK.10` is never examined as a match at all — `needs == ["OPIK.3"]`. Before the change, `_ID_TOKEN.findall` over that same group returned both `OPIK.3` and `OPIK.10`. So a genuine `Needs <known-id>` phrase is silently lost (the very failure the feature is meant to prevent: the conflict detector cannot protect that task), while the test suite only covers phrases separated by newlines (`OPIK.9`) where `finditer` can restart.

The `known`-membership guard only prevents ids nobody wrote; it does nothing about ids written in a non-dependency role.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new clamp `clause = re.split(r"[.;:]\s", m.group(1), maxsplit=1)[0]` is not applied to a sentence — `_PROSE_DEP`'s `(.{0,200})` capture is up to 200 characters of the *paragraph* after the keyword, and `finditer` skips everything the match consumed. Two concrete inputs go wrong:

1. Keyword directly followed by a colon. For `- [ ] **OPIK.20** Needs: OPIK.3.` (OPIK.3 declared earlier, so it is in `known`), `m.group(1)` is `": OPIK.3."`; `re.split(r"[.;:]\s", ...)` splits at the colon because it is followed by a space, so `clause` becomes `""`, `_ID_TOKEN.findall("")` returns nothing, and `OPIK.20.needs == []`. Before this change the same input produced `needs == ["OPIK.3"]` (the old code scanned all of `m.group(1)`), so this is a regression: `Requires: OPIK.3`, `Needs: OPIK.3` and `Depends on: OPIK.10` are all silently dropped.

2. A second dependency phrase later in the same paragraph is swallowed by the first match. For `- [ ] **OPIK.21** Depends on OPIK.3. Needs OPIK.5.`, the match on `Depends on` consumes `" OPIK.3. Needs OPIK.5."` (no newline, under 200 chars); the clamp keeps only `" OPIK.3"`, and because `finditer` resumes *after* the consumed match, the `Needs OPIK.5` keyword is never seen again — `needs == ["OPIK.3"]`, `OPIK.5` is lost. Pre-change both ids were reported.

Both cases silently under-report needs — the exact failure class this change exists to fix (a missing need means the task is never marked blocked and the conflict detector cannot protect it), and neither case is covered by the added tests, which only exercise a later sentence that contains no dependency keyword (`Related: see OPIK.3`).
